datasets.label: Simulated corona · January 2008
datasets.title: ε Eridani’s corona in a published simulation, for its magnetic field of January 2008
datasets.description: Nobody has imaged this corona. This is the gas density in the magnetohydrodynamic simulation Ó Fionnagáin, Kavanagh, Vidotto et al. (2022), ApJ 924, 115 ran for this star, driven by the map of its surface magnetic field observed in January 2008 (Jeffers et al. (2014), A&A 569, A79), from the data they released (https://zenodo.org/records/5575241). The released state is ten minutes after the authors set off an eruption near the equator of the model; that eruption disturbs 6% of the volume drawn here. It is shown the way coronagraph pictures are: at each distance from the star brightness is proportional to the density there, and only the steep fall-off with distance is compressed. The rotation axis is tilted 46° from the line of sight, as the magnetic maps were fitted; these sources give neither where the axis points on the sky nor the star's rotation phase today, so both are drawn by convention.
datasets.summary: A published simulation, not an image: gas shaped by the magnetic field mapped in January 2008.
datasets.detail: 96³ grid from 5.1 million simulation cells, 1 to 4 stellar radii

facts.label: Kind
facts.value: A published simulation driven by an observed magnetic map, not an observation

facts.label: Magnetic map
facts.value: January 2008, from spectropolarimetry (Jeffers et al. (2014), A&A 569, A79)

facts.label: State
facts.value: Ten minutes after a modelled eruption near the equator, which disturbs 6% of the drawn volume

facts.label: Density at 2 radii
facts.value: Typically 1.2 × 10^7 electrons per cm³; the densest twentieth is 10 times the thinnest

facts.label: Orientation
facts.value: Rotation axis 46° from the line of sight, as the maps were fitted; its direction on the sky and the rotation phase are conventions

facts.label: Brightness
facts.value: Proportional to density at each distance; 10 times the typical density is fully bright. The fall-off with distance is compressed (log₁₀ density, 1.0 × 10^5 to 1.0 × 10^9 cm⁻³)

datasets.label: Modelled wind · measured mass loss
datasets.title: ε Eridani’s corona as the wind that carries its measured mass loss
datasets.description: Nobody has imaged this corona. This is the density of the wind Parker (1958) derives for gas at 4.06 million kelvin, the temperature measured from the star's X-ray spectrum, carrying 30 times the Sun's mass loss, which Wood et al. (2002) measure from the star's astrosphere. It leaves the surface at 93 kilometres a second and passes the speed of sound 1.89 radii out. It is the same in every direction, because the model has no magnetic field; the simulated datasets show what the field does to it.
datasets.summary: Modelled, not observed: the outflow at the measured temperature that carries the measured mass loss.

facts.label: Kind
facts.value: A model from published numbers, not an observation

facts.label: Mass loss
facts.value: 30 times the Sun's, measured from the astrosphere (Wood et al. 2002)

facts.label: Temperature
facts.value: 4.06 million K, measured from the X-ray spectrum (Bennedik et al. 2026)

facts.label: Density at the surface
facts.value: 6.2 × 10^7 electrons per cm³

facts.label: Density at 4 radii

facts.label: Brightness
facts.value: log₁₀ density, 1.0 × 10^5 to 1.0 × 10^9 cm⁻³, in the star's color
